utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could the registrar please read the case number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-13a-T. The Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume the appearances are as -- no, today we should have the appearances probably. For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Mr. Niemann, and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm Toma Fila. With me are Mr. Petrovic and Mr. Kostic, Defence team of Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me? Thank you. Before we start, let me report to you that in probably one hour, or in a few minutes, we will receive a copy of the reports from the medical officer and from the commanding officer of the detention unit about Mr. Dokmanovic. It will be, of course, provided to both parties and the court. After hearing the witnesses, I suggest that if we have time, we should go through the list of exhibits prepared by the court deputy, Mr. Bos, to discuss the various matters he rightly raised in his letter of the 12th of June. One final point. I suggest that tomorrow, when we resume our hearings, we should move to Courtroom 1, which is available, because I think it is quite appropriate for the closing statements of the parties to be held in a bigger courtroom. I suggest that we start tomorrow, if it is agreeable to both parties, at 9.00 instead of 9.30. All right. Any comments or suggestions or any housekeeping matters? So we can start with the first witness for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it closed session already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand you would like to go into a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I had asked the registrar and also the Defence whether it's possible, and if Your Honours would agree with that, because it is a UN person, and New York had only agreed to him testifying under very restrictive provisions as to his anonymity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. I see the Defence counsel is not objecting to your request, so we are going into closed session. It is Witness S?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Witness S, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, were you able to find your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Somewhere there to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a brief summing up of Witness S, I would like to formally tender this statement. I think it was just marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Actually, yes, I thought it had been tendered already because I saw Mr. Fila hinting that he -- nodding that he had no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but his nodding wasn't registered in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think, Mr. Fila, that we don't have any document, a statement from, of course, the present witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He is an investigator from my team, and I have quite a few of his reports. And you can accept them and, on the other hand, you don't have to accept them, but it's a good thing for you to see them any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, are you an investigator of my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm the investigator of the Defence team in the Slavko Dokmanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I shall be showing you a few documents now, and you are going to tell me what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could the usher please show him the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this is, the documents that we're going to show you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D153, and the English translation D153A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are these actually two reports that you submitted to me at my request?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are two reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please tell me which the first one is and what the first one is about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: It concerns this case, but I see that in one of the reports here, a page is missing or at least I didn't get a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's some kind of mistake. We'll see what it is all about.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: It is the report that speaks about the video cassettes that I collected and the conversation with Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Only one was translated, but you will also mention the other, won't you? Those are the statements in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please come over again?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D154 and the English translation D154A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D155, the English translation D155A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Obviously your report is related to this other matter and hasn't been translated, Tomasevic Vukosav, this is -- Mr. Vasic, did you at my request, under my instructions, first talk to the witnesses that were already heard by this court, Mirko Dragisic and Vukosav Tomasevic, and then you went to see them and you took from both of them respectively copies of the video cassette that they got from Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the Prosecutor denied the authenticity of the tape and the segment of the tape that is registered at 15.42, under the instructions of Mr. Dokmanovic's Defence attorney, I got in touch with these witnesses, namely, Mr. Mirko Dragisic and Mr. Vukosav Tomasevic, who had testified before this court, and then I went to see them. And in their statements, they said that they each had a copy of the tape that has been registered as D2 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did they receive these copies of this videotape and from whom?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: They got these copies in 1991 from Mr. Nebojsa Lazarevic who was also a witness before this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they confirm this to you under oath?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: They did, and this is contained in their signed statements underlining that they were under the oath, the solemn oath, that they took before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I now ask you to look at these two video cassettes, and could you please mark which one you got from whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could this also be admitted into evidence as two different Defence exhibits, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The videotapes are marked D156 and D157.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You will tell us about D156, who it belongs to and who gave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: D156, video cassette D156, I received from Mr. Tomasevic, and that is the cassette that he got, as he said, in 1991. And he confirmed that on it is a recording which is identical to the one that he obtained on that day and that he gave to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the other cassette?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: The other cassette, D157, was given to me by Mr. Mirko Dragisic also with the statement that he received this cassette in 1991 and that it is now identical to the tape that he got in 1991. That is the same tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And both are copies?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, both are the copies of the tape made by Mr. Novakovic which was made on the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Nebojsa Lazarevic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Nebojsa Lazarevic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At this point in time, I wish to have this admitted into evidence or to play these tapes so that you could see that they are the same like D2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we haven't seen them so we object, because we haven't seen them. So we can't agree to something we haven't seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's why I asked, yes. So I asked whether you want to have them played. If you want to have them played so that you could see them, certainly we shall play them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not sure that will necessarily remove our objection. I would like to see them. We may need to look at them overnight and just make sure that we are happy with them. Watching them on the television in the courtroom for the first time may not be sufficient for that purpose. I think the best course would be for us to uplift them and have a look at them overnight, rather than trouble the court with them now. I also have an obligation with the statements but I will raise those matters when they are sought to be tendered, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know if I understood this correctly. Mr. Niemann would want to take these tapes to have a look at them overnight and then to say tomorrow whether he objects to having them admitted or not? Fine, fine, that's fine. So let us just mark them for identification and then tomorrow we'll decide on that, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we will put it off until tomorrow morning when the Prosecution will let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As regards to the witness statements and the reports, is it all right to have this admitted into evidence today or do you want to take a look at all of this and then say tomorrow whether you agree to it or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, this is the first time I have seen these. I know of no notion of the oath sort of extending beyond the Tribunal to someone who's spoken to at some subsequent stage. My concern about this is that the witnesses were here and available for cross-examination, Witness Q, and certainly all these questions could have been presented then, I would have thought. At this stage, tentatively, I'm not so concerned about the issue of the videotape. I would like to consider it overnight and then make a decision tomorrow morning as to whether we have any objection to the statement which merely says the videotape was given to them in 1991 and this is the tape that's now tendered. I don't think I have much difficulty with that, but I'm hoping that I can accommodate that and agree to the tender of this. But I certainly would object to the Witness Q statement. It goes into a whole range of other matters, and I don't believe that this is the effective way or proper way of doing it. I object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honours, just a brief explanation. As regards to the existence of these tapes, when the witnesses were heard before this honourable court, they said that they received these tapes. And Nebojsa Lazarevic stated that he gave them copies so the question was tackled in cross-examination. However, the core of the matter now is that they did not have the tapes with them on that occasion, because it was not necessary for them to bring them in. And only on the 29th of May, Mr. Williamson, the Prosecutor, contested these tapes. It is only then that I instructed Mr. Vasic to take the tapes from the witnesses under oath. It would have been a different situation if the witnesses were to come again just to tell you, "Yes, that is the tape." So the matter of the tape was mentioned in their testimony, and it is contained there. That is one thing. Secondly, I have nothing against discussing this issue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I think this would be the best course of action, again, to put off until tomorrow the question of whether or not they may be tendered in evidence. All right. I confirmed that we will then decide tomorrow morning, in light of any comments or objections from the Prosecution, about both the videotapes, the two videotapes, 156, 157, and the witness statements, D154 and D155. This will be decided tomorrow. Whereas for the report by the Defence team investigator marked as D153, the court considers that it can't be admitted into evidence, this is the report about Witness Q, for the reasons explained by the Prosecution. So it will be marked only for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It will just be admitted, yes, fine. What I wish to say, Your Honour, let me be quite clear: If the Prosecutor is against this, I will have to have these witnesses called back. I am going to have a delay and also going to incur immense expenses to have them brought in here and say, "Yes, this is my tape," and that is what they are going to say because these are their tapes. That is what I wish to say on that question. And now I kindly ask the usher to show another document to the investigator so that he could tell us what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just respond to that, Your Honours. That is the reason why I am going to see if I can possibly accommodate those statements merely to get the videotapes in, as videotapes that they had at the time. So I just want to consider it, but I would try and do that, because I can understand it may necessitate having to call the witnesses, and I don't want to do that or cause that to happen, although that was the issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked D158.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Something else, Your Honour, in order to clarify matters for Mr. Niemann. The tapes I'm talking about are copies of the tape that is the original Defence Exhibit, so this is yet another generation, if that's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, could you please tell us what this is about and why you took this statement from Mr. Novakovic who was already heard as a witness before this court?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: This statement was taken as a supplementary one from Mr. Novakovic after Mr. Curtis, the investigator for the Prosecution, was heard before this court. Because in his notes, he mentioned something that witness Novakovic did not say here before this Trial Chamber, bearing in mind the fact that Mr. Novakovic, in his conversation with me, told me that while he was talking to Mr. Curtis he drank alcohol. I went under the instructions of the Defence attorney to discuss that particular matter with him, because this was a completely new set of circumstances in relation to what he had testified to before this court. And during our conversation, he told me that Mr. Curtis came to see him and that after walking into his office, he told the secretary to bring in a bottle of whiskey, and that he drank this whiskey while he was giving his statement. He also said that he was not informed that notes would be taken, and nobody asked him to read anything out or to sign it. And he thought that would be only natural because he, himself, says that he was under the influence of alcohol at that point in time. He also told me that after this conversation with Mr. Curtis and an interpreter from Macedonia, and also an investigating judge from Backa Palanka, he went to a restaurant near the bridge, because Mr. Curtis wanted him to go to the bridge, to see the bridge. So then they went to a restaurant and they all drank alcohol together. That is basically the content of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you also talk to the secretary? Did she confirm that she brought the drinks in?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: I only discussed that particular matter with her, and she corroborated that, that she indeed did bring in the bottle of whiskey, and that when she came back, the bottle was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who drank that whiskey?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: She didn't know. And Mr. Novakovic, he told me that he was drinking alcohol, but he didn't say anything about Mr. Curtis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The next thing I wish to ask you about, Mr. Vasic -- oh, yes. If there are no objections, I move that this be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I wish to consider this matter and to consult with Investigator Curtis about the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Niemann, it's a terribly peripheral issue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. That is why I will endeavour to determine whether I will agree to it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Again, we will wait for your consultation with Mr. Curtis --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- before deciding on this matter. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, for the purposes of the Defence, did you also go and talk to certain persons who were related to the event that occurred in Ovcara on the 20th of November, 1991, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Since October 1997, at the request of the Defence attorney, I went out and tried to find persons who had some knowledge about the questions related to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you made a report about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I made a report about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you gave it to me, and I handed it in. Could you please tell me, what does this report say? What did you talk about? To whom?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: In the report, I processed conversations with persons who did not want to make statements. In one case, a person did not even want to say his name and surname. I talked to a gentleman who is marked as Witness Q, and the Defence attorney told me that he is Witness Q, and in my papers, I have his full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at a piece of paper, and I'm going to write down a name and surname, and you will tell me whether that is Witness Q or not.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D159 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the person concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it is that person. The first word written herein is the nickname of the person in question. I would like to have this marked as a Defence Exhibit for identification purposes and to confirm that it has been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what did this person tell you in the course of that interview when the interview took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honours. Your Honours, we have here a situation, as far as I understand, of a person who refused to testify, and the investigator goes and has a conversation with him and then seeks to come here and give evidence of the conversation. Your Honours, there is no opportunity to cross-examine, we don't know this person, and it's entirely objectionable, Your Honours. If the witness fails to come, there are many means which can be explored to get witnesses to testify before this Tribunal that doesn't involve them coming to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no, no, please, Your Honours, there's something wrong. Let me clarify. This is not the witness that has not testified here. We're talking about a witness that has testified here before the court. There has been a misunderstanding. This person testified as a Defence witness, that's the Witness Q. So the objection by Mr. Niemann concerns something completely different. I don't know what it concerns. The person whose name you read has testified before this court as Witness Q. This is the person we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. It has been pointed out that the name shown on the piece of paper would appear to be some sort of a nickname. That's why I didn't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It doesn't affect my objection. It still stands in the sense that again we have a situation of a witness who apparently was here and could have testified to these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It doesn't assist, and it's inappropriate, in my submission, for the investigator to go out and have a subsequent conversation and then attempt to relate what was the content of that investigation. I mean, if Mr. Fila is prepared to give me a transcript of what was said in it, in a similar vein to the issue raised by Judge May, it may be a matter of such little significance that to us it doesn't matter. So as to avoid any delay in the proceedings or matters like that, we may agree to it being admitted, if that's what the Defence feels important. But it would only be on that basis. It wouldn't be on the basis that, in my submission, it is admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not clear here again. There has been a misunderstanding. First of all, I submitted the report. You have it in front of you. I did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann. We have received D153A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then it's in there. We're talking about the witness who testified here, he was questioned here, just as Mr. Curtis talked to Witness Novakovic. If this is to be a fair trial, my investigator has the right to talk to a Defence witness, and he talked before that with him with their permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours have ruled the report inadmissible, and now it's sought to get the material and the evidence into evidence by means of this witness testifying. I mean, if Your Honours have ruled the report inadmissible, then surely this witness is not to be permitted to testify as to those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have decided to confirm our ruling that this statement D153A, the English version, should not be admitted into evidence for the reasons stated before. However, that for reasons of fairness, the witness should be allowed to be examined and cross-examined on the substance of this statement, and, of course, it will be for the court then to decide what probative value to attach to his testimony. So therefore, Mr. Fila, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before I continue, one other matter. Witness Q was asked the question, I asked him the question, and you will find in his statement that he confirmed that he had talked to the investigator, that he talked to the Defence team. You have this in Witness Q's statement, and that's the reason why I brought here this witness, the investigator, with whom Witness Q confirms that he talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Vasic, can you tell us, what did you talk about and what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: First, I have to say that I talked with Witness Q on the 1st of October, 1997, so when he was not a witness yet, and at the very beginning of the conversation, he told me that he did not wish to testify, to be a Defence witness, since he wanted to live in Vukovar in Republic of Croatia and that that would cause him problems, and if he decided to testify, he would prefer to testify as a Prosecution witness. Then he told me briefly how he happened to find himself in the area caught up in war. I don't know whether the Defence is interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it any different from what he testified to before the court?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Well, afterwards, I saw the statement that he gave to the Prosecutor and his testimony, the transcript of his testimony, and what he told me does not differ from what he said to the Prosecutor and before this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are there any differences?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a difference. I think only in his formulations, in the wording, and at one point, there is a difference in where he found Witness Berghoffer and Witness Perkan. He did not say the full name of that person. As to where he found Mr. Berghoffer, he said that he does not remember whether it was on the bus or at the route, at the strip, but he said that it was impossible to do that in the hangar because nobody could take anyone out of the hangar. He gave me an illustration. He said that he had singled some people out, a group of people out. He asked whether he could do that. He asked Miroljub Vujovic whether he could do that, and he said yes, and later on he presumed that these people were killed. So that's one of the differences. Another difference concerns Mr. Dokmanovic. When I asked him whether he saw Mr. Dokmanovic on the 20th of November when he was at Ovcara, he said that Mr. Dokmanovic was not there, at least not while this witness was there, and he said that he would have seen him had he been there because he knew him as a former President of the Municipal Assembly in Vukovar and that it was his opinion that Mr. Dokmanovic was not allowed to go there, he would not dare to go there, because he was considered as a traitor by extremist Serbs, and that even the witness thought him a traitor, and that he probably would have been killed had he appeared at Ovcara. I then asked Witness Q why he thought Dokmanovic to be a traitor, and he told me that it was because he handed Vukovar over to the Croats and that allegedly, on the 2nd of May, after the attack on Borovo Selo, he called in the army and thus saved those Croats who were in a bad situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The other persons that you talked to refused to testify, so we cannot discuss them. Only if maybe the Prosecutor will be interested to know who these persons are, maybe you can then assist him. I would now like the Trial Chamber to allow me to show the witness a document that he has brought in. This has not been translated. But he will read a few important sentences and that will make it possible for you to understand what this is all about until the full translation is available. Can you please tell us, where did you get this document and tell us what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D160.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you please read? That's the decision of which court? What is this about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: This is a decision of the County Court in Osijek, and this is a decision to the effect that the sentence of imprisonment pursuant to the final judgement of the County Court in Osijek, number was mentioned, of July 1992, this sentence was quashed. The accused, Borislav Bugunovic, Mladen Hadzic, Goran Hadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Vitomir Devetak, Dragan Sabljakovic, Slavko Dokmanovic, Vojislav Susa, Mladen Jovic, Ilija Petrovic, Milan Knezevic, Borivoj Milinkovic, Paji Medic, Bogdan Vorkapic, Caslav Ocic, Miomir Crnogorac, Stevi Bogic, Ilija Koncarevic, Dordu Latas, Caslav Niksic, and Radmil Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are these mostly the members of the government?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: I think that's the full cabinet of the District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's the government in which Slavko Dokmanovic was the Minister of Agriculture?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the Croatian court does not prosecute him for anything?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This document I received while I was in Vukovar. In June, I got it from a colleague of mine, Vojislav Ore, who is also an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to have this document admitted as a Defence Exhibit, and the translation will be admitted once it's finished. What number is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have to object a document that's not translated, I can't submit comment on it, but I also, based on what's been said about the document, wonder what its relevance is. But until I've read it, I can't comment any further, Your Honours, on it, other than object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, this is a judgement. Maybe there has been a misunderstanding. This is a final judgement of the court whereby the sentence of imprisonment, ten years' imprisonment, against Slavko Dokmanovic has been quashed, and there are no proceedings being conducted against him before Croatian courts, so this is a final judgement. I can't see how a final judgement of a court cannot be admissible. There is a signature there, there is the stamp of the -- that's the County Court. And by this judgement, the whole government of the Serbian district and Slavko Dokmanovic have been amnestied, pardoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the Prosecutor is right in saying that we can't admit into evidence a document which is not either in English or in French, in one of the two working languages, official languages, of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Then we will wait. You said that I can submit, with the approval of the court, documents in the original language. I did not have enough time to have it translated because Mr. Vasic arrived yesterday. When the translation service finishes the translation, then it's okay. This is a document -- this does not testify to the guilt of Mr. Dokmanovic, but it more goes to the sentencing procedure. It shows what his status in Croatia is. And you said in your brief that I can submit such documents in the original language, and that's Croatian. Once it's translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The registry may provide the translation by tomorrow morning because we can then again discuss this document tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's a very brief document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: They are mostly names. Mr. Bos, do you think we can?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I'll bring it to the translation unit right now, and then hopefully we will have a translation tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And finally, the last document I wish to tender is in English. This hasn't been translated into Serbian, but that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what is it that you brought with you from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked D161.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I could give you this document in the original size, but, please, give me back one of the smaller copies then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you give this to me?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's an article from the Washington Post dated 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How is Mr. Dokmanovic addressed here?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: As a former mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to have this document admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I find it surprising, Your Honour, that Mr. Fila would seek to tender newspaper articles bearing in mind the fate of a newspaper article that I sought to tender at one stage and Your Honours ruled to be inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's an article published in the newspapers. It's again important for what Mr. Dokmanovic said in 1993. I saw a lot of such exhibits from the Prosecutor, interviews on tape. That's the same thing. That's the Washington Post dated 1993, so it could not have been in anyone else's hands, and he is described as the former mayor of Vukovar. It can be an exhibit that will go to the sentencing or whatever. We had several newspaper articles admitted into evidence whose substance was not contested. I think that it should be admitted into evidence because it speaks to the personality of Mr. Dokmanovic, and that's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, the document that I sought to tender did exactly the same thing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I agree with you. Of course, we consider that newspaper articles normally are not reliable because they can't reflect accurately the reality, but I wonder, Mr. Niemann, whether, for -- if it is admitted only for sentencing purposes, you would still object?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's what I want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was the basis on which I sought to tender mine, Your Honours, partly for that reason, I must admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Only for sentencing purposes. Let me make this clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have decided to admit it into evidence and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This will be D161. All right. Thank you. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, what time of the day was it when you saw Witness Q?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon. I can't recall the exact time, but it was in the afternoon, around 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where in the hotel did you conduct the interview with him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: I talked to him in the restaurant of the hotel located -- the restaurant is on the first floor just as you climb the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there anyone else present with you during the course of the interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vladimir Petrovic was also present during the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who asked the witness questions? Was it you or you and Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: I mostly asked the questions of the witness, as far as I can remember. Whether Mr. Petrovic asked any questions, well, it's possible, but I can't tell you that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you take notes of the interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I took notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they hand-written notes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, hand-written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you now have those notes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Will you produce them for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: They're here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps they could be handed with the assistance of the usher who doesn't seem to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If you allow me, the notes regarding this conversation or the notes in their entirety? Because several people were interviewed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just want to see the notes that he made of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I take it these notes are in the Serbian language, are they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I interviewed this witness in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: All of the notes are taken down by yourself, are they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: As you can see, the handwriting is the same throughout, so I took all those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't see that because there is some handwriting in blue ink on the last page which looks like a list of names. It may be the same handwriting, but it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: You're reading the back side of this statement which relates to a list of witnesses and telephone numbers which has nothing to do with my testimony, and you're not interested in this. And I think it's not really fair that you should read this. However, let me clarify in relation to your remark. This was written down in a ball-point pen. You can check whether the handwriting is the same. You have handwriting experts for that, but this is all in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What questions did you actually put to Witness Q? What did you say to him? And try, if you would, to be as precise as possible in advising us of the questions you asked according to the way you asked them, rather than just as a general summation of what was said.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Niemann, you probably are aware that I cannot give you the precise wording of the questions because a long time has passed for me to be able to remember precisely what I asked. I think that no one here in this courtroom would be able to do that. I have to tell you one thing: Before interviewing Witness Q, I did not have a lot of information or an idea of what really happened on the 20th of November, 1991. So I just initiated the discussion, and then he, Witness Q, told me what he had to tell me. I did not have enough information to ask any questions of him before he told me his story. The only thing that I did ask is, after his story, I asked him concrete questions about Slavko Dokmanovic, whether he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was on the 1st of October, 1997? I need to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the 1st of October, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it's not information that was given to you after the Prosecution led any rebuttal evidence. This is information that was given to you before, as far back as 1997?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Since the 1st of October, 1997, I have not seen Witness Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Fila about what Witness Q had told you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally, I told Mr. Fila what Witness Q had told me after the interview. That's the reason why Mr. Fila asked the questions that he did in the course of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever make any attempt to contact Witness Q after he had testified in the proceedings to ask him why he had testified the way he did?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, from my report, which has not been admitted here, it is quite clear that, during the first interview, Witness Q told me that he did not wish to testify as a Defence witness. So any further attempts to contact this witness would be in vain, so that's the reason why I did not contact him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Didn't you find it surprising that Witness Q didn't testify to these matters when he came to the -- to all of these matters when he came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: I don't know in which sense. What do you mean, "surprising"? I simply talked to the witness and took down what he told me, and I did not enter into any discussions as to what he would be testifying about or not. But when I saw his statements in his statement given to the Prosecutor, he more or less repeated what he had told me. Why he repeated that or did not repeat that in front of the court, I would not like to enter into that. That is for the Trial Chamber and the parties to discuss. What he told me was not different to any considerable extent than what he told the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say that he failed to disclose to the Prosecutor and the Prosecutor's investigator and to the Trial Chamber certain details about Slavko Dokmanovic and they were simply omitted -- although it was simply omitted from the statement. Now, I'm saying, isn't that surprising? Wasn't that surprising to you as the investigator that that had happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: I did not say that he did not give the details concerning Slavko Dokmanovic. On the contrary, I said that he did even here before the court when he testified, but he did not present them in the same form in which he gave them to me, that information. Witness Q here stated that he did not see Mr. Dokmanovic on that day at Ovcara, and he had told me that he had not seen him there. Of course, while Witness Q was there, as you know, according to his statement, he went back to Ovcara three times. He was at Ovcara three times, so he went back twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But that's the point, isn't it, that you knew that he had said to you that he had gone back twice on previous occasions? Isn't that the difference? Or perhaps you might be able to help me --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: I never claimed that that was the difference. This is in my report. That's what he told me too. The only difference is in the wording. He said that he did not see Mr. Dokmanovic on that day and he had told me that he had not been there. And had he been there, he would have been killed because Serbian extremists thought him to be a traitor. I don't see a difference, the difference that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when he told you this, that he considered that Mr. Dokmanovic wouldn't have been there because he was a traitor and would have been killed, did you ask him why it was that this view of him was held? Did you go into that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: I asked him, as I have already stated before the court, why did he think Mr. Dokmanovic to be a traitor. And he told me, to repeat what I have already said, for two reasons: One is that he handed Vukovar over to Croats; and the other was that allegedly after the 2nd of May, after the conflict in Borovo Selo, he called in the army units and by doing that, he somehow saved the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he tell you who he considered -- did he tell you which Serbs it was that considered him to be a traitor? Did he give you any names?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: He told me that these were extremist Serbs. I assume that these would be those Serbs who were members of the TO and volunteers, as he said, and who were at Ovcara on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's merely an assumption on your part, though. You don't know for sure that's what he was referring to, those are the people he was referring to when he said that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: He did not tell me that precisely, so you're right. This is my assumption. He merely spoke about extremist Serbs. I should not be testifying about assumptions, but only about things that I have heard. But I have to say that he did tell me that Dokmanovic would have been killed had he come to Ovcara. So you can make your own conclusions, what context this sentence was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Petrovic ask him any questions that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: I can't remember really. I allow that it's possible but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With Mr. Niemann's permission, I could ask one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whether Witness Q mentioned whom he saw at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But first let me check whether Mr. Niemann agrees with that question. If he objects, then I will not ask this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you object?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead and answer, because these are those people who refused to testify. You will hear now why they refused to testify.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: May I answer, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, during our conversation, he did mention some persons who were there and whom he saw. He mentioned Miroljub Vujovic, Stanko Vujanovic, Ivica Husnik. He mentioned also -- well, it's a problem because my notes are with the Prosecutor so I can't remember all those names. Jankovic; he mentioned, furthermore, Toma Cigan, Cetin (phoen) and several other names. I really can't remember. After all those years, I can't remember those names. I've got my notes and the Prosecutor has my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Maybe the Prosecutor could be so kind to hand the notes to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you later on talk to these people and did they tell you what happened there and why they refused to testify?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: May I answer this question, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: After that, I met some of these people. None of them, naturally, wanted to give me a statement. They claimed that they did not want to do so because they feared criminal prosecution, not all of them. When I talked to Mr. Vujovic, he refused to tell me anything, anything specific about Ovcara. And he also didn't want to tell me why he refused to talk to me about that. When I talked to Mr. Husnik, he quoted the reason that I just stated as the reason why he refused to give me a statement. He was there at the day when Witness Q claims that he was there. I don't know whether it would be necessary for the court for me to give you the substance of our discussions, since this person was not here and he did not testify. He is not a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might I just have the notes back again, Your Honours? I wish to have them read to me in the English language so that I can understand them, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder whether copies could be made because this is an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can uplift them from the registrar if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I forgot to ask the witness about an entire segment. So with your permission, it's not too long, can I ask him now? I'm sorry. I shall really try to be short.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you go to Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I asked for your permission because there's no point not having this recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you go to Vukovar, according to my instructions, to see the places marked by Mr. Dzuro as the probable places that were filmed at 15.42?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Vukovar and Negoslavci at the request of the Defence attorney. And I wish to thank this honourable court for the permission they gave me, because, had it not been for that, I wouldn't have received a visa from the Croatian authorities. I stayed in Vukovar, and I was at the place that the Prosecutor stipulated as the place where the 15.42 recording is on the D2 tape. So that is the house for which the Prosecutor claims is in Vukovar. After that, I went through the entire area of Negoslavci, but because of the lush greenery in the month of June just before summer starts, I did not manage to reliably ascertain what is the exact place that is depicted on the videotape at 15.42. But you will agree with me that one cannot preclude the possibility of what Mr. Dzuro said. Certainly that possibility cannot be precluded, that that place is precisely the one that was marked by Mr. Dzuro. But, on the other hand, I tried, by resorting to empirical methods, to check the materials I got or, rather, that the Defence got from the Prosecutor. But for want of technical means, which we regrettably do not have, I could not get valid results. But I consulted the School of Forestry, the university, after we heard Mr. Tabbush, and they told me that Mr. Tabbush's conclusion is probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After that, did you feel it necessary to talk on the phone or in other ways with the witnesses who were in those two vehicles, and did any one of them tell you whether there was this possibility of them returning or something?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, again, I object to this testimony. This is going to the central point. If this evidence is sought to be led, then the Prosecution, Your Honour, would ask that the witnesses testify to these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is a sound objection, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry. No problem. I withdraw the question. I was just -- I was just trying to be helpful to the court. The answer would have been more useful to you than to me, but I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann, you are entitled to cross-examination, if any, about these last questions put by Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I do have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, did you look out for things other than just vegetation when you went to the scene which is depicted at time 15.42 on Exhibit D2, such as the house, sign posts, sheds, poplar trees and walnut trees, things of that nature? Did you look out for matters such as that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, I was looking for that, and there is no doubt about it. That is why I went there. And when I talked about vegetation, I was saying that it made it rather difficult for me to come to the right conclusions. Of course, on the one hand, I looked for the house that would correspond to the house that one can see at 15.42 on the tape, although you cannot really see it very well on the tape, and that is why I wanted to see that part of the landscape that would correspond to the tape. I agree with you that the main characteristics of this area are the sign post, then the house on the right-hand side of the pole. By then, I heard about the poplar and the apple tree from Mr. Tabbush, so I saw that too. And if we are talking about the place that Mr. Dzuro talked about, that is, the place that is in Vukovar, I found the pole. But in my assessment, it is much closer to the right-hand side of the road, the curb, the one that you can see at 15.42. The vegetation at that place is lush and, therefore, you cannot recognise it, generally speaking. Another thing I was looking for was the sign post, but it was not there. I also noticed a small house which is at that particular place, but I cannot say whether it corresponds to the house on the tape at 15.42, because if I were to present my opinion, it would only be my opinion; and in my opinion, that is not it, but that doesn't have to mean anything. As far as the poplar tree is concerned, it is there. I already mentioned the walnut tree. At the School of Forestry at the university, they told me that it was quite probable that the conclusion of Professor Tabbush is right. As far as the house is concerned, it, according to its colour -- rather, the colour of its bricks, would match those colours, and also some of its structural characteristics would be similar. But, again, I cannot say whether they're the same house or not. I was not sure because I could not see it properly on the tape itself. So all these elements that you mentioned, I did look for.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you're far too modest. Your opinion, I'm sure, would assist us. Do you feel that the position that was depicted by Mr. Dzuro as being the correct spot on 15.42 of D2 was, in fact, the right spot? And your opinion will do fine.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Well, as a witness, I did not want to present opinions before the Trial Chamber, but if you ask me to do so, I will tell you what I think about it. I think that that place perhaps does look like the place that is registered at 15.42, but to my mind, what would not be identical is the pole on the right-hand side of the road, the distance between it and the road, and also the fact that a sign post is not there. So there is no intersection on the right-hand side. And I don't know whether, in that situation, there would be any need to have a sign post there. The little house that is there, it seems to me, is much more fragile than the house that one can see in the back. It's a white house, you know. I always thought that it was a house that was made out of solid construction materials, but no. And as regards the house on the left-hand side which, by its volume and its bricks, would perhaps match the one, the angle that the camera had at 15.42 is an angle that I simply could not see, that I simply could not get, because the walnut tree is in front and it is green. And now it is enormous as opposed to the autumn when the recording was made in 1991. So I could not get the same visual effect in order to draw a comparison. That is why I talked about vegetation. However, according to its size and colour, the house could be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And no doubt you went down and checked out the scenery around Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And had you found a place that resembled the spot at 15.42 in Negoslavci, you would have been very quick to come before this Tribunal and tell us about that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV VASIC
utterances.text: I presented before the court everything I saw and heard, and I certainly would have said that too. But then I will tell you another thing. In Negoslavci, there is also a house that, according to size and the colour of its bricks, does match this house. But the landscape, at least under the circumstances that I saw it in this situation, would not correspond to the ones we saw on the tape. Perhaps in the autumn it looks different, but under these conditions, I did not have the impression that that was the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. I assume there's no objection to the witness being released. Mr. Vasic, thank you so much for coming to give evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The pleasure was mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, may I suggest that we quickly go through the two items I raised this morning at the outset; namely, first of all, I wonder whether the reports submitted by the medical officer and the commanding officer have been, yes, filed? All right. So we can get a copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, may I address the court? I was informed by the Dutch police that their report -- remember the famous report that we've been looking for for the past year? It should be in the registry by noon today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Report about what? About the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The tape, the videotape. The videotape that the Dutch police -- the Prosecutor was kind enough to establish this contact for me, and they were supposed to have this done by noon today, reportedly so. I kindly ask that we look at it tomorrow as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course. Yes. But I had understood from Mr. Williamson that the Dutch police had refused to draw up a report because this was a copy, so they were unable. Probably I was under a misunderstanding. Anyway, we are going to receive this report --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There are two things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Anyway, we will receive this report, and it will be discussed tomorrow. Now, what about the letter now, the issues raised by Mr. Bos in his letter of the 12th of June about some exhibits? Mr. Bos points out that Prosecutor's Exhibits 103A, 104A, 105A, 106A, and 196A, as well as 199A, are still to be tendered to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, an error, Your Honour. They were to be provided in English translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. We can hand them up now. I think this is 103A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 104, 105, 106, 196, and 199. I assume they had already been provided in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 196 we have, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, but not a final version, apparently it was a draft translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. All right. Now then, Prosecutor's Exhibits 138, 139, and 169.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They are available too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Available to the registry. These are for the registry. According, again, to Mr. Bos, Defence documents 115 to 125, plus 127 and 209, were marked for identification on the 27th of May, but a decision on their admission was postponed until an English translation was available. Now, the translation I understand will be ready by Monday, the 22nd. Well, this was said on the 12th of June. So probably it is available, this translation, I imagine, and I wonder whether the Prosecutor can tell us whether or not they object to the tendering of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we haven't seen the translation. Again, I can't imagine that there will be an objection but, again, without having seen the English translation, I'm in some difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Bos, whether the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Well, the translations were provided to Defence counsel on Monday, it's a Defence Exhibit, so since they were marked for identification only, I have left it to the Defence to submit the documents, and I don't know whether they are intending to do that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the afternoon, we are going to give all these copies to the Prosecutor. We just have to make a sufficient number of copies. You will receive them in the afternoon and you will say what you have to state about that tomorrow in the context of anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are there any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is one more matter. During the course of evidence, Your Honours, of the -- excuse me, Your Honour. I just had to check something, Your Honour. During the testimony of Witness Mesic, he produced two exhibits, I believe, Exhibits P108 and P111, and there are mentioned, in both the documents, attachments. We sought to obtain from the United Nations in New York copies of the attachments because they weren't attached to his copy of the letters. A search of the Security Council archives has failed to provide us with the attachment to Exhibit P111, but we have the attachment to P108. That has been sent over from New York. In fact -- and I make that available, Your Honours, to the Chamber. I provide the whole of the document we received from New York -- in fact, the first page is repetitious of Exhibit P108 -- but I think it's probably helpful if, Your Honour, it could all be attached because this is presumably the Security Council's copy of the document that was sent by Mr. Mesic. So that was something we had undertaken to do. We didn't succeed with 111, but we did with P108. So if that could be attached as P108A or B, whatever is convenient to the register?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I'll mark it as P108A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any other matter? Yes, Mr. Niemann, you have other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Your Honours moved on to the other exhibits before we had finished, so I'll just hand all of these, I think, to the registrar, if I may? These are the ones mentioned in paragraphs 1 and 2 of the memorandum of the registrar. They are the English translations of all of them. I hadn't completed handing them all up, but they are all here, and if I may give them all to the registrar? Perhaps he could be kind enough to attach them. Finally, Your Honours, as mentioned yesterday, instead of calling Professor Wagenaar, we would tender his report and his curriculum vitae. They are available, and I seek to do that now, and ask that they be marked the next Prosecution Exhibit number in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We already had yesterday the agreement of Mr. Fila, yes, to its being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement will be marked 262.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the CV.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the CV, 263.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think I'm through, Your Honour. These are the documents in paragraph 2, paragraph 2 of Mr. Bos's memorandum of the 12th of June. I think, Your Honour, that disposes of all matters that were outstanding so far as the Prosecution is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I just kindly ask Mr. Niemann whether there is something that I haven't received out of all of this so that I won't have to go through all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. These are the English translation. Mr. Fila would have received the original document in the first place, but he probably doesn't have the translations so if --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So copies of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I don't need the translations into Serbian. That's okay. But I was just wondering, what did you get from New York? Is it something that I haven't seen yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do apologise. Yes, indeed, it is, and I do apologise to Mr. Fila. I should have made it available to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I want to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I don't press to tender it at this stage until Mr. Fila has had a chance to read it. I do apologise, Mr. Fila, for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as for the closing statement, we are grateful to Mr. Fila for providing the court with the Serbian text. Now, Part A has already been translated. I understand we will receive the remaining part of the translation tomorrow morning. What about the Prosecution? Of course, this has been sent only to us, not to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, this afternoon, Your Honour, we're expecting to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, there is an attachment, which may not be ready, which is more by way of assistance to Your Honours in just locating where pieces of evidence are. I'm not sure when that is going to be available. But the whole -- the rest of it is available, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We can rise now, and we will reconvene tomorrow at 9.00 in the big courtroom, Courtroom 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 12.00 p.m. to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of June, 1998 at 9.00 a.m.
